songs.title: You’re No Good
songs.note: Written by the Californian blues and one-man-band performer Jesse Fuller, it opens Dylan's first album, played on acoustic guitar and harmonica.
songs.preview: A man complains, half in fun, about a woman who has done him nothing but wrong.

songs.title: In My Time of Dyin’
songs.note: A traditional gospel blues best known from Blind Willie Johnson's 1927 recording, which Dylan sings with slide guitar on his first album.
songs.preview: A dying man asks for the comfort of his faith and to be laid to rest in peace.

songs.title: Man of Constant Sorrow
songs.note: A traditional Appalachian song popularised by the Stanley Brothers; Dylan's early arrangement appears on his 1962 debut album.
songs.preview: A wanderer who has known nothing but trouble says farewell to his home and the people he loved.

songs.title: Fixin’ to Die
songs.note: A Delta blues written and first recorded by Bukka White in 1940, given a ferocious, gravel-voiced reading on Dylan's first album.
songs.preview: A man who senses death is close worries less about himself than about the children he will leave behind.

songs.title: Pretty Peggy‐O
songs.note: A traditional ballad descended from the Scottish song The Bonnie Lass o' Fyvie, which Dylan sings in a playful, exaggerated style on his debut.
songs.preview: A soldier courts a girl in a town his company passes through, and the story ends with his death.

songs.title: Highway 51
songs.note: Adapted from Curtis Jones's 1938 Highway 51 Blues, it is a fast, hard-strummed road blues on Dylan's first album.
songs.preview: A man stands by a long southern highway, thinking of the woman who left along it and the road that may carry him too.

songs.title: Gospel Plow
songs.note: A traditional spiritual, also sung as Keep Your Hand on the Plow, given a fast, raucous treatment on Dylan's first album.
songs.preview: A short, driving spiritual urging the faithful to keep working toward heaven and not look back.

songs.title: Baby, Let Me Follow You Down
songs.note: A traditional blues Dylan says in its spoken introduction he learned from Ric Von Schmidt in Cambridge; he later played it electric with the Hawks in 1966.
songs.preview: A man pleads with a woman to let him go wherever she goes, promising to do anything for her.

songs.title: Freight Train Blues
songs.note: An old country song recorded by Roy Acuff among others; on Dylan's first album it is a fast yodelling showcase with one famously long held note.
songs.preview: A man born to the railroad says he cannot rest, because the sound of a passing freight train always calls him away.

songs.title: See That My Grave Is Kept Clean
songs.note: Written and recorded by Blind Lemon Jefferson in the late 1920s, it closes Dylan's first album as a slow, solemn blues.
songs.preview: A dying man's single last request is that his grave be looked after once he is gone.

songs.title: Down The Highway
songs.note: A Dylan original on The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan, a solo acoustic blues written while his girlfriend Suze Rotolo was away studying in Italy.
songs.preview: A man whose lover has gone far across the sea takes to the highway, lonely and unsure she will return.

songs.title: Bob Dylan's Blues
songs.note: A short comic song on The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan, opened by a spoken introduction poking fun at songs written in Tin Pan Alley.
songs.preview: A light, rambling joke song about the singer going his own way and keeping clear of fads and fakes.

songs.title: Talking World War III Blues
songs.note: A talking blues on The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan, in the comic spoken style of Woody Guthrie, about a dream of surviving a nuclear war.
songs.preview: A man tells a doctor about his dream of wandering an empty city after the bombs, and finds everyone else has the same dream.

songs.title: Corrina, Corrina
songs.note: A traditional blues first recorded in the late 1920s, it is the one track on The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan with a backing band.
songs.preview: A man misses the woman who has gone and says he cannot rest until she comes back to him.

songs.title: Honey, Just Allow Me One More Chance
songs.note: A fast, comic song on The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan, adapted from a 1920s recording by the songster Henry Thomas.
songs.preview: A man begs a woman for just one more chance, in a lighthearted song that never quite sounds heartbroken.

songs.title: I Shall Be Free
songs.note: The closing track of The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan, a rambling comic song loosely modelled on Lead Belly's We Shall Be Free.
songs.preview: A string of tall tales and jokes about politicians, women and celebrities from a singer who insists he will be free.

songs.title: All I Really Want to Do
songs.note: The opening track of Another Side of Bob Dylan; the Byrds and Cher both released versions in 1965.
songs.preview: A man assures a woman that he wants nothing from her except friendship, with no demands and no games.

songs.title: Black Crow Blues
songs.note: A slow blues on Another Side of Bob Dylan, notable as one of the album's tracks on which Dylan plays piano rather than guitar.
songs.preview: A lonely man waits and frets for a woman who has gone, uneasy and unable to settle.

songs.title: Spanish Harlem Incident
songs.note: A short love song on Another Side of Bob Dylan, later recorded by the Byrds on their 1965 debut album.
songs.preview: A man is dazzled by a gypsy woman he meets in the city and asks her to tell him who he is.

songs.title: I Shall Be Free No. 10
songs.note: A comic follow-up to I Shall Be Free from Freewheelin', it sits in the middle of Another Side of Bob Dylan.
songs.preview: A rambling, joking song in which the singer mocks himself, his critics and the world around him.

songs.title: To Ramona
songs.note: A gentle waltz on Another Side of Bob Dylan, with a lilting, Mexican-flavoured rhythm on acoustic guitar.
songs.preview: A man tenderly tells a troubled woman she is being misled by others and should trust her own way.

songs.title: Motorpsycho Nitemare
songs.note: A comic talking song on Another Side of Bob Dylan that parodies the old farmer's daughter joke and Hitchcock's film Psycho.
songs.preview: A traveller asks for a bed at a farmhouse and ends up fleeing a farmer, his daughter and a shotgun.

songs.title: I Don’t Believe You (She Acts Like We Never Have Met)
songs.note: A song from Another Side of Bob Dylan that he later transformed into a loud electric number on his 1966 tour with the Hawks.
songs.preview: A man is baffled that a woman he spent a night with now behaves as though she has never seen him.

songs.title: Ballad in Plain D
songs.note: A long confessional ballad near the end of Another Side of Bob Dylan, about the end of his relationship with Suze Rotolo; he later said he regretted it.
songs.preview: A man recounts the bitter end of a love affair, the quarrels around it, and the guilt and freedom left behind.

songs.title: One Too Many Mornings
songs.note: A quiet acoustic song from The Times They Are a-Changin' that Dylan later turned into a loud full-band number on his 1966 tour.
songs.preview: A man stepping away from a lover at daybreak admits that neither of them is wrong, yet he cannot stay.

songs.title: North Country Blues
songs.note: A ballad in the voice of a woman from an iron-mining town, drawing on the Minnesota iron range where Dylan grew up.
songs.preview: A miner's widow traces how her town and family fall apart as the mines close and the work goes overseas.

songs.title: She Belongs to Me
songs.note: The second track on Bringing It All Back Home, played softly by a small electric band; Rick Nelson recorded it in 1969.
songs.preview: A portrait of a self-possessed artist woman who belongs to no one, watched by a man half in awe.

songs.title: Outlaw Blues
songs.note: A rough electric blues on the first side of Bringing It All Back Home, the rock-and-roll half of the album.
songs.preview: A restless, rough-edged blues in which the singer casts himself as a hunted man who trusts nobody.

songs.title: On the Road Again
songs.note: A fast electric blues near the end of side one of Bringing It All Back Home.
songs.preview: A man lists the absurd horrors of his girlfriend's household and wonders why she expects him to move in.

songs.title: Bob Dylan's 115th Dream
songs.note: Closes the first side of Bringing It All Back Home and opens with a false start that collapses into laughter before the band comes in.
songs.preview: A sailor's absurd dream of landing in America and being met by a parade of rude, ridiculous Americans.

songs.title: It Takes a Lot to Laugh, It Takes a Train to Cry
songs.note: A slow piano blues on Highway 61 Revisited; an earlier, much faster version was recorded under the title Phantom Engineer.
songs.preview: A weary traveller, borne along by a train through the night, longs to be with the woman he loves.

songs.title: From a Buick 6
songs.note: A fast twelve-bar blues near the end of the first side of Highway 61 Revisited.
songs.preview: A man in a hard, dangerous life praises the one woman who looks after him and will stand by him.

songs.title: Pledging My Time
songs.note: The second track on Blonde on Blonde, a slow Chicago-style blues led by harmonica.
songs.preview: A man in a bad way promises his devotion to a woman and hopes she will come through for him.

songs.title: One of Us Must Know (Sooner or Later)
songs.note: Closes the first side of Blonde on Blonde and was the only track on the album recorded in New York rather than Nashville.
songs.preview: A man explains to a former lover that he never meant to hurt her and that their whole affair was a misunderstanding.

songs.title: Leopard-Skin Pill-Box Hat
songs.note: A twelve-bar Chicago-style blues on side two of Blonde on Blonde, released as a single in 1967.
songs.preview: A jilted man mocks the trendy hat his former girlfriend wears and the new man she has taken up with.

songs.title: Most Likely You Go Your Way and I'll Go Mine
songs.note: Opens the third side of Blonde on Blonde; Dylan and the Band played it to open their 1974 tour, heard on Before the Flood.
songs.preview: A man tells a lover who has deceived him that they are better off going their separate ways.

songs.title: Temporary Like Achilles
songs.note: A slow piano blues on the third side of Blonde on Blonde.
songs.preview: A man shut out by the woman he wants complains that she keeps him waiting while another stands guard over her.

songs.title: Absolutely Sweet Marie
songs.note: An upbeat organ-driven rocker on the third side of Blonde on Blonde.
songs.preview: A man stuck waiting for an absent woman wonders where she is and why she has left him hanging.

songs.title: Obviously Five Believers
songs.note: A fast Chicago-style blues that closes the third side of Blonde on Blonde, listed on the album as Obviously 5 Believers.
songs.preview: A man pleads with his baby to come back to him as soon as she can, promising to be waiting.

songs.title: The Ballad of Frankie Lee and Judas Priest
songs.note: The longest song on John Wesley Harding, a parable sung over a sparse acoustic backing that ends with a plainly stated moral.
songs.preview: Two friends, one a tempter, test each other over money and desire in a parable that ends in a death.

songs.title: Dear Landlord
songs.note: Built around Dylan's piano, it sits on the second side of John Wesley Harding; Joe Cocker recorded it in 1969.
songs.preview: A man asks the landlord who holds power over him not to judge him too harshly or reduce him to what he owes.

songs.title: I Am a Lonesome Hobo
songs.note: A short, sombre story-song on the second side of John Wesley Harding.
songs.preview: A wandering hobo confesses the greed and crimes that brought him low and warns others to live better.

songs.title: I Pity the Poor Immigrant
songs.note: Its tune is close to the Scottish folk song Come All You Tramps and Hawkers; Joan Baez recorded it on her 1968 album Any Day Now.
songs.preview: A grave lament for a newcomer whose greed and selfishness leave him empty even in a land of plenty.

songs.title: Down Along the Cove
songs.note: The second-to-last track on John Wesley Harding, one of two bright country love songs that close the album with pedal steel guitar.
songs.preview: A happy man walks by the water with the woman he loves and everyone can see how good they are together.

songs.title: Peggy Day
songs.note: A light, jaunty love song that closes the first side of Nashville Skyline, sung in the soft croon that marks the whole album.
songs.preview: A playful, grinning tribute to a girl the singer is glad to spend his days and nights with.

songs.title: One More Night
songs.note: An upbeat country song on the second side of Nashville Skyline, following Lay Lady Lay, with a brisk shuffle under a lonely lyric.
songs.preview: A man alone under the night sky mourns a woman who has left him and wonders how he failed her.

songs.title: Country Pie
songs.note: One of the shortest songs on Nashville Skyline, running under two minutes, it sits just before the closing Tonight I'll Be Staying Here with You.
songs.preview: A rollicking celebration of simple pleasures, using a list of fruit pies as a happy stand-in for country music and life.

songs.title: Time Passes Slowly
songs.note: One of the songs Dylan wrote in 1970 for Archibald MacLeish's play Scratch, it became the third track on New Morning.
songs.preview: A reflection on quiet country days, where time seems to stand still and the singer is content to stay put.

songs.title: Went to See the Gypsy
songs.note: A piano-led New Morning song set in a hotel, often read by listeners as a veiled account of a meeting with Elvis Presley.
songs.preview: A traveller goes to see a famous fortune-teller in a big hotel, but the encounter slips away like a dream.

songs.title: Winterlude
songs.note: A crooned waltz on New Morning, its old-fashioned melody recalling the softer singing Dylan had used on Nashville Skyline.
songs.preview: A sweet, old-fashioned winter romance in which the singer invites his sweetheart to enjoy the snow and each other.

songs.title: If Dogs Run Free
songs.note: A jazzy New Morning track that Dylan half-recites over a loose cocktail-lounge band, with a woman's wordless scat singing weaving around him.
songs.preview: A musing on freedom and acceptance, asking why we should not let all creatures, and ourselves, live as we please.

songs.title: New Morning
songs.note: The title track of the album, written for Archibald MacLeish's play Scratch, it is one of the most joyful songs Dylan recorded in this period.
songs.preview: Waking to a bright country morning, the singer rejoices in nature, renewal and simply being with the one he loves.

songs.title: Sign on the Window
songs.note: A slow piano ballad near the middle of New Morning, often counted among the album's finest and most personal songs.
songs.preview: After a lonely winter and a broken romance, the singer imagines settling down to a quiet family life.

songs.title: One More Weekend
songs.note: A bluesy, good-natured rocker on New Morning, one of the album's few uptempo numbers.
songs.preview: A husband begs his wife to slip away with him for a weekend alone, leaving the children and everyday life behind.

songs.title: Three Angels
songs.note: A spoken-word piece on New Morning, Dylan reciting rather than singing over organ and a soft gospel-style chorus.
songs.preview: Three angel decorations look down over a busy city street while ordinary people hurry past without noticing them.

songs.title: Father of Night
songs.note: The closing track of New Morning, a short piano hymn also written for Archibald MacLeish's play Scratch; Manfred Mann's Earth Band later recorded an extended version.
songs.preview: A brief, intense prayer praising God as the maker of night and day, of love and of the whole natural world.

songs.title: Alberta
songs.note: A traditional folk blues that Dylan recorded in two versions, Alberta #1 opening Self Portrait and Alberta #2 closing it.
songs.preview: A man calls out to a woman named Alberta, longing for her and wondering where she has gone.

songs.title: I Forgot More Than You’ll Ever Know
songs.note: A country song written by Cecil Null and a 1953 hit for the Davis Sisters, which Dylan recorded in Nashville for Self Portrait.
songs.preview: A jilted lover tells the new partner of his former sweetheart that he knows her far better than they ever will.

songs.title: Days of 49
songs.note: A traditional ballad of the California Gold Rush, credited on Self Portrait as arranged by Alan Lomax, John Lomax and Frank Warner.
songs.preview: An old prospector looks back on the wild days of the gold rush and the rough companions now long gone.

songs.title: Early Mornin’ Rain
songs.note: Written by Gordon Lightfoot and recorded by Ian and Sylvia and Peter, Paul and Mary before Dylan cut it for Self Portrait.
songs.preview: A broke, stranded man at an airport watches a plane take off toward home, unable to follow it.

songs.title: In Search of Little Sadie
songs.note: The first of two versions of the traditional murder ballad on Self Portrait, its tempo and key lurching unpredictably from verse to verse.
songs.preview: A man shoots a woman named Sadie, flees across the country, and is caught and brought to trial.

songs.title: Let It Be Me
songs.note: An English version of Gilbert Bécaud's French song Je t'appartiens, made famous by the Everly Brothers in 1960 and recorded by Dylan for Self Portrait.
songs.preview: A tender plea from a lover who asks to be the one person their beloved always turns to.

songs.title: Little Sadie
songs.note: The second, straightforward version of the traditional murder ballad on Self Portrait, played at a brisk, even pace.
songs.preview: The killer of a woman named Sadie tells of his crime, his flight and his capture and sentence.

songs.title: Woogie Boogie
songs.note: A short instrumental on Self Portrait, a loose boogie-woogie jam credited to Dylan.
songs.preview: A brisk, good-time boogie-woogie romp led by rolling piano and a bright, bouncing band.

songs.title: Belle Isle
songs.note: A traditional ballad from the British Isles and Newfoundland, recorded by Dylan for Self Portrait with strings added afterwards.
songs.preview: A returning young man tests his sweetheart's faithfulness while in disguise, then reveals himself when she stays true.

songs.title: Living the Blues
songs.note: A Dylan original that he performed on The Johnny Cash Show in 1969 before recording it for Self Portrait.
songs.preview: A man left behind by his love confesses that he has been sinking into sadness ever since she went away.

songs.title: Gotta Travel On
songs.note: A folk song adapted by Paul Clayton and a 1959 hit for Billy Grammer, recorded by Dylan for Self Portrait.
songs.preview: A restless man feels the pull of the road and knows he must leave town and keep moving.

songs.title: Blue Moon
songs.note: Written by Richard Rodgers and Lorenz Hart in 1934 and recorded by countless singers before Dylan crooned it on Self Portrait.
songs.preview: A lonely singer sees his life changed when the moon that watched over his solitude suddenly brings him love.

songs.title: Take Me as I Am (or Let Me Go)
songs.note: A country ballad written by Boudleaux Bryant and a hit for Ray Price, which Dylan sings in a soft Nashville style on Self Portrait.
songs.preview: A man asks his lover to accept him exactly as he is, or else to set him free.

songs.title: Take a Message to Mary
songs.note: Written by Felice and Boudleaux Bryant and first a hit for the Everly Brothers, it appears on Self Portrait as a close-harmony country cover.
songs.preview: A man locked away for his crimes asks a friend to hide the truth from the woman he loved.

songs.title: It Hurts Me Too
songs.note: An old blues long associated with Tampa Red and Elmore James, which Dylan recorded for Self Portrait as a quiet, mostly acoustic performance.
songs.preview: A man watches the woman he loves suffer at the hands of another, and feels her pain as his own.

songs.title: Wigwam
songs.note: A Dylan instrumental on Self Portrait, carried by a wordless hummed vocal and a slow horn arrangement, later heard in the film "The Royal Tenenbaums".
songs.preview: A lazy, hummed melody drifts over brass, a song without words that feels like a half-remembered tune.

songs.title: Sarah Jane
songs.note: A traditional-based song recorded in Dylan's 1970 sessions and released on the 1973 album "Dylan", with female backing singers.
songs.preview: A cheerful man sings of his devotion to Sarah Jane and the happy, crowded home they share.

songs.title: Mr. Bojangles
songs.note: Written by Jerry Jeff Walker and later a hit for the Nitty Gritty Dirt Band, it was released on "Dylan", the album Columbia assembled from outtakes.
songs.preview: A narrator remembers meeting an old wandering dancer in a jail cell who told the story of his life.

songs.title: The Ballad of Ira Hayes
songs.note: Written by Peter La Farge and made famous by Johnny Cash, it tells the true story of a Pima Marine who helped raise the flag on Iwo Jima.
songs.preview: A Native American war hero comes home to neglect and drink, and dies forgotten by the country that praised him.

songs.title: Mary Ann
songs.note: A traditional folk song of a sailor's farewell, recorded by Dylan around 1970 and released on the 1973 Columbia album "Dylan".
songs.preview: A man about to sail away mourns the woman he must leave behind on the shore.

songs.title: Big Yellow Taxi
songs.note: A cover of Joni Mitchell's 1970 song, recorded by Dylan in his sessions of that era and released on the 1973 album "Dylan".
songs.preview: A bright, catchy complaint that we only value the natural world, and the people we love, once they are gone.

songs.title: A Fool Such as I
songs.note: Written by Bill Trader and a hit for both Hank Snow and Elvis Presley, it was recorded by Dylan around Self Portrait and released on "Dylan".
songs.preview: A jilted man admits he is still devoted to the woman who left him and will go on loving her.

songs.title: Spanish Is the Loving Tongue
songs.note: A cowboy song set to a poem by Charles Badger Clark, which Dylan recorded more than once; this version is on the 1973 album "Dylan".
songs.preview: A cowboy remembers a Mexican girl he once loved and lost, and still hears her tender words.

songs.title: Main Title Theme (Billy)
songs.note: The instrumental that opens the soundtrack to Sam Peckinpah's film "Pat Garrett and Billy the Kid", built on the melody of the album's song "Billy".
songs.preview: A spare acoustic theme sets a lonesome frontier mood, circling slowly as if over open country.

songs.title: Cantina Theme (Workin’ for the Law)
songs.note: An instrumental from the "Pat Garrett and Billy the Kid" soundtrack, its subtitle pointing to Garrett's turn from outlaw to lawman in the film.
songs.preview: A relaxed, slightly uneasy groove plays like music heard in a frontier saloon.

songs.title: Bunkhouse Theme
songs.note: A short acoustic instrumental from the soundtrack to "Pat Garrett and Billy the Kid".
songs.preview: Gentle interlocking acoustic guitars play a quiet, homely tune, like evening music in a cowboy bunkhouse.

songs.title: River Theme
songs.note: An instrumental from the "Pat Garrett and Billy the Kid" soundtrack, featuring wordless voices over a slow, flowing accompaniment.
songs.preview: Wordless singing floats over a slow, gentle melody that moves like water drifting past.

songs.title: Turkey Chase
songs.note: A lively instrumental from the "Pat Garrett and Billy the Kid" soundtrack, driven by fiddle and banjo in an old-time country style.
songs.preview: Fiddle and banjo race along in a bright, rollicking old-time tune full of chase and fun.

songs.title: Final Theme
songs.note: The instrumental that closes the soundtrack album for "Pat Garrett and Billy the Kid", returning to the film's mournful main melody.
songs.preview: A slow, stately farewell melody brings the story to a sorrowful close.

songs.title: Going, Going, Gone
songs.note: A slow song from Planet Waves, recorded with The Band, notable for Robbie Robertson's stinging guitar answering Dylan's voice.
songs.preview: A man who has reached the end of something resolves to walk away and leave it all behind.

songs.title: Tough Mama
songs.note: A driving rock song on Planet Waves, recorded with The Band in Los Angeles in late 1973.
songs.preview: A man pays tribute to a strong, earthy woman who inspires him and pulls him back into the world.

songs.title: Hazel
songs.note: A short love song from Planet Waves, recorded with The Band, which Dylan also performed with them in "The Last Waltz".
songs.preview: A man longs for a woman named Hazel and asks her to give him a little of her love.

songs.title: Something There Is About You
songs.note: A love song from Planet Waves, recorded with The Band, in which Dylan refers to his boyhood in Duluth, Minnesota.
songs.preview: A woman stirs up memories of his youth and a feeling he cannot name, and he pledges himself to her.

songs.title: Dirge
songs.note: One of the starkest songs on Planet Waves, performed only by Dylan on piano and Robbie Robertson on acoustic guitar.
songs.preview: A man looks back with bitterness and self-disgust on a consuming attachment he is finally ready to leave.

songs.title: You Angel You
songs.note: A cheerful, mid-tempo love song from Planet Waves, recorded with The Band.
songs.preview: A man is so smitten with a woman that he can think of nothing else and calls her an angel.

songs.title: Never Say Goodbye
songs.note: A tender love song from Planet Waves, recorded with The Band, set against an image of a wintry northern landscape.
songs.preview: Amid a frozen winter scene, a man asks the woman he loves never to leave him.

songs.title: You’re a Big Girl Now
songs.note: The third track on Blood on the Tracks, and one of the five songs he re-recorded in Minneapolis in December 1974 for the final album.
songs.preview: A man tells a woman who has moved on without him that he sees her growing and wishes he could change.

songs.title: Meet Me in the Morning
songs.note: A slow twelve-bar blues that opens the second side of Blood on the Tracks, kept from the New York sessions of September 1974.
songs.preview: A weary man asks a woman to meet him at dawn so they can leave together, though he senses she may not come.

songs.title: If You See Her, Say Hello
songs.note: The eighth track on Blood on the Tracks, re-recorded in Minneapolis in December 1974; the earlier New York take had a harsher, more wounded tone.
songs.preview: A man asks a friend to pass his greetings to the woman who left him, hiding how much he still misses her.

songs.title: Odds and Ends
songs.note: The opening track of The Basement Tapes, a short, fast rocker recorded with the Band near Woodstock in 1967.
songs.preview: A man gives up on a careless partner whose broken promises and wasted chances have finally worn out his patience.

songs.title: Orange Juice Blues (Blues for Breakfast)
songs.note: A Richard Manuel song performed by the Band without Dylan, one of the Band-only tracks added to the 1975 release of The Basement Tapes.
songs.preview: A lonely man nurses the blues over breakfast, missing a woman who has gone and dreading the long day ahead.

songs.title: Million Dollar Bash
songs.note: A Basement Tapes party song recorded with the Band in 1967; Fairport Convention released a cover on their 1969 album Unhalfbricking.
songs.preview: A crowd of oddballs and misfits all gather and stumble toward one wild, enormous party.

songs.title: Yazoo Street Scandal
songs.note: A Robbie Robertson song performed by the Band without Dylan, added to the 1975 release of The Basement Tapes.
songs.preview: A rowdy tale of a young man drawn into trouble by a dangerous woman on a disreputable street.

songs.title: Goin’ to Acapulco
songs.note: A slow, mournful song from the 1967 Woodstock sessions with the Band, first released on The Basement Tapes in 1975.
songs.preview: A tired man heads off to Acapulco to see a woman for some fun, though his voice carries more sorrow than pleasure.

songs.title: Katie’s Been Gone
songs.note: A Richard Manuel and Robbie Robertson song performed by the Band without Dylan, added to the 1975 release of The Basement Tapes.
songs.preview: A man mourns a woman who has left, wondering how long he can stand her absence.

songs.title: Lo and Behold!
songs.note: A comic travelling song from the 1967 Woodstock sessions with the Band, first officially released on The Basement Tapes in 1975.
songs.preview: A restless traveller hops from town to town, meeting strange people and leaving each place with a shout.

songs.title: Bessie Smith
songs.note: A Rick Danko and Robbie Robertson song performed by the Band without Dylan, added to the 1975 release of The Basement Tapes.
songs.preview: A tribute to the great blues singer Bessie Smith, looking back at her world with affection and longing.

songs.title: Clothes Line Saga
songs.note: A deadpan story song from the 1967 Woodstock sessions, often heard as a reply to Bobbie Gentry's "Ode to Billie Joe".
songs.preview: A family takes in the washing and trades flat small talk while big news passes by almost unnoticed.

songs.title: Apple Suckling Tree
songs.note: A nonsense song in nursery-rhyme style, recorded with the Band near Woodstock in 1967 and released on The Basement Tapes in 1975.
songs.preview: A playful, nonsensical rhyme about meeting someone under a tree, sung for the joy of the sound.

songs.title: Please, Mrs. Henry
songs.note: A comic barroom song from the 1967 Woodstock sessions with the Band, first officially released on The Basement Tapes in 1975.
songs.preview: A drunk, broke man begs a woman named Mrs. Henry to help him out of his sorry state.

songs.title: Too Much of Nothing
songs.note: Written and recorded at the 1967 Woodstock sessions with the Band; Peter, Paul and Mary released it as a single later that year.
songs.preview: A brooding warning that emptiness and idleness can make people cruel, restless and lost.

songs.title: Yea! Heavy and a Bottle of Bread
songs.note: A nonsense song from the 1967 Woodstock sessions with the Band, first officially released on The Basement Tapes in 1975.
songs.preview: A jumble of absurd images about packing up and setting off, sung with a straight face.

songs.title: Ain’t No More Cane
songs.note: A traditional prison work song about convict labour, performed by the Band without Dylan on the 1975 release of The Basement Tapes.
songs.preview: Prisoners describe the brutal, endless labour of cutting cane under guard, and long for it to be over.

songs.title: Crash on the Levee (Down in the Flood)
songs.note: Recorded with the Band in 1967; he re-recorded it as "Down in the Flood" for Bob Dylan's Greatest Hits Vol. II in 1971.
songs.preview: With the water rising and the levee about to break, a man warns a woman she will have to fend for herself.

songs.title: Ruben Remus
songs.note: A Richard Manuel and Robbie Robertson song performed by the Band without Dylan, added to the 1975 release of The Basement Tapes.
songs.preview: An upbeat, good-time Band number built around a colourful, restless character.

songs.title: Tiny Montgomery
songs.note: One of the earliest songs from the 1967 Woodstock sessions with the Band, first officially released on The Basement Tapes in 1975.
songs.preview: A roll call of oddball characters, all told to pass the word that Tiny Montgomery is coming back.

songs.title: Don’t Ya Tell Henry
songs.note: A Dylan song performed by the Band without him on the 1975 release of The Basement Tapes.
songs.preview: A comic, rowdy tale of a night of mischief that the singer keeps insisting must be hidden from Henry.

songs.title: Nothing Was Delivered
songs.note: Recorded with the Band near Woodstock in 1967; the Byrds recorded it for their 1968 album Sweetheart of the Rodeo.
songs.preview: A man demands that someone explain why nothing they promised ever arrived, and own up to it.

songs.title: Open the Door, Homer
songs.note: A loose, rambling song from the 1967 Woodstock sessions with the Band, first officially released on The Basement Tapes in 1975.
songs.preview: A man asks a friend to let him in while sharing odd bits of advice about living and forgiving.

songs.title: Long Distance Operator
songs.note: A Dylan blues performed by the Band without him on the 1975 release of The Basement Tapes.
songs.preview: A desperate man pleads with a telephone operator to put his call through to the woman he loves.

songs.title: Mozambique
songs.note: Written with Jacques Levy, this short, breezy song sits in the middle of Desire and was also released as a single.
songs.preview: A light invitation to a sunny faraway coast where couples dance and fall in love.

songs.title: Romance in Durango
songs.note: Written with Jacques Levy, it is one of the long story songs on Desire, with a chorus sung partly in Spanish.
songs.preview: An outlaw flees across Mexico with the woman he loves, haunted by the man he has killed.

songs.title: New Pony
songs.note: The opening track of Street-Legal, a heavy blues with the album's gospel-style backing singers answering him throughout.
songs.preview: A sultry, menacing blues in which a man sings about a pony as a thinly veiled stand-in for a lover.

songs.title: No Time to Think
songs.note: One of the longest songs on Street-Legal, a slow waltz packed with abstract nouns and symbolic figures.
songs.preview: A man caught among temptations, duties and lost loves finds he never has a moment to stop and reflect.

songs.title: Baby Stop Crying
songs.note: Released as a single from Street-Legal, it is a slow ballad with the album's gospel-style backing singers.
songs.preview: A man tries to comfort a heartbroken woman and offers to help her if she will let him.

songs.title: True Love Tends to Forget
songs.note: A mid-tempo song on the second side of Street-Legal, built around a hooky chorus with the backing singers.
songs.preview: A man worn down by an unsteady love asks his partner not to deceive him or let him go.

songs.title: We Better Talk This Over
songs.note: A late track on Street-Legal, a brisk breakup song set to the album's horns and backing singers.
songs.preview: A man suggests to his partner that their relationship is over and they should part without bitterness.

songs.title: Where Are You Tonight? (Journey Through Dark Heat)
songs.note: The closing track of Street-Legal, a long, dense song that ends the album on a note of hard-won survival.
songs.preview: A man searching for a lost lover through a dark, dreamlike night comes out the other side changed.

songs.title: Do Right to Me Baby (Do Unto Others)
songs.note: A gentle, mid-tempo song on Slow Train Coming built around the Golden Rule from the Gospels.
songs.preview: The singer refuses to judge or harm others and asks only to be treated the way he treats them.

songs.title: A Satisfied Mind
songs.note: Written by Red Hayes and Jack Rhodes and a 1955 country hit for Porter Wagoner, it opens Saved as a short gospel-style performance.
songs.preview: Wealth cannot buy contentment, and a peaceful heart is the only thing worth taking to the grave.

songs.title: Covenant Woman
songs.note: A slow ballad on Saved that blends a love song with a song of faith.
songs.preview: The singer thanks a woman who has shared his faith and stands beside him in a covenant with God.

songs.title: What Can I Do for You?
songs.note: A slow gospel song on Saved, notable for an extended harmonica solo, one of the few on his gospel records.
songs.preview: A grateful believer, aware of all that has been given to him, asks God what he can offer in return.

songs.title: In the Garden
songs.note: A dramatic gospel song on Saved about the life of Jesus, often used to close his gospel-era concerts.
songs.preview: Retelling moments from the life of Jesus, the song asks whether the people around him truly saw who he was.

songs.title: Saving Grace
songs.note: A slow, hymn-like song on the second side of Saved.
songs.preview: A humble believer marvels that he has been kept alive and rescued by grace he did not earn.

songs.title: Are You Ready
songs.note: The closing track of Saved, a gospel song with a call-and-response between Dylan and his backing singers.
songs.preview: The singer asks, again and again, whether the listener is prepared to meet God when the end comes.

songs.title: Heart of Mine
songs.note: Released as a single from Shot of Love, it is a loose, rolling love song rather than a gospel one.
songs.preview: A man warns his own heart not to give itself away to a woman who will only hurt him.

songs.title: Property of Jesus
songs.note: A hard-edged rock song on Shot of Love, mixing the album's faith themes with sharp defiance.
songs.preview: The singer defends a believer from the mockers around him, insisting he belongs to Jesus and cannot be bought.

songs.title: Watered‐Down Love
songs.note: An upbeat song on Shot of Love, with a light, bouncy groove and backing singers.
songs.preview: True love is pure, patient and selfless, quite unlike the weak and grasping imitation people settle for.

songs.title: The Groom's Still Waiting at the Altar
songs.note: First issued as a B-side, this hard-rocking song was added to later editions of Shot of Love.
songs.preview: A man searches for a vanished woman in a world that seems to be falling apart around him.

songs.title: Dead Man, Dead Man
songs.note: A mid-tempo song on Shot of Love with a lightly reggae-flavored rhythm.
songs.preview: The singer confronts a spiritually dead man, perhaps his own old self, and asks when he will finally rise.

songs.title: In the Summertime
songs.note: A gentle, reflective ballad near the end of Shot of Love, with harmonica.
songs.preview: Looking back on a summer long ago, the singer remembers a love or grace that changed him.

songs.title: Trouble
songs.note: A blues on Shot of Love, placed just before the closing song, Every Grain of Sand.
songs.preview: Trouble is everywhere, in every street, home and institution, and nobody can escape it.

songs.title: Man of Peace
songs.note: A Dylan original that opens the second side of Infidels, set to a loping, bluesy groove carried by the Sly Dunbar and Robbie Shakespeare rhythm section.
songs.preview: A warning that evil rarely announces itself and may arrive looking like a gentle, trustworthy peacemaker.

songs.title: Seeing the Real You at Last
songs.note: The opening track of Empire Burlesque, a Dylan original that sets the album's bright, horn-and-drum-machine production from its first bars.
songs.preview: A lover who has finally seen through a partner's act and feels relieved, even liberated, to be done with the illusion.

songs.title: I'll Remember You
songs.note: The second track on Empire Burlesque, a Dylan original and one of the album's slower, more tender songs, later a regular in his concerts.
songs.preview: A promise to keep a lost lover in memory long after everything else has faded and the road has moved on.

songs.title: Clean Cut Kid
songs.note: A Dylan original first tried during the Infidels sessions and finished for Empire Burlesque, a sardonic rocker about a young American soldier of the Vietnam era.
songs.preview: An ordinary, all-American boy is sent to war and comes home a broken stranger whom no one understands.

songs.title: Never Gonna Be the Same Again
songs.note: A Dylan original from Empire Burlesque, a soft soul-pop ballad built around backing singers and a smooth mid-1980s production.
songs.preview: A brief encounter with someone has changed the singer for good, and he admits there is no going back.

songs.title: Trust Yourself
songs.note: A Dylan original from Empire Burlesque, a funky, chant-like rocker driven by a repeated title hook and loud mid-1980s drums.
songs.preview: Advice to rely on your own judgment rather than on preachers, lovers, experts or anyone else claiming to know best.

songs.title: Emotionally Yours
songs.note: A Dylan original from Empire Burlesque, a slow piano-led love ballad later recorded by the O'Jays as the title track of a 1991 album.
songs.preview: A heartfelt declaration that, whatever happens, the singer belongs to his lover body and soul and will stay that way.

songs.title: Something's Burning, Baby
songs.note: A Dylan original from Empire Burlesque, a dark, slow-marching song that stands out on the album for its ominous drum-led arrangement.
songs.preview: A lover senses that something has gone badly wrong between them and pleads for honesty before it is too late.

songs.title: You Wanna Ramble
songs.note: The opening track of Knocked Out Loaded, a cover of a rhythm and blues number credited to Herman Parker Jr., the Memphis singer known as Junior Parker.
songs.preview: A man warns a restless lover that if she wants to run around, she should not expect him to wait at home.

songs.title: Precious Memories
songs.note: A gospel hymn written by J. B. F. Wright in the 1920s and widely sung in Southern churches; Dylan recasts it with a lilting, Caribbean-flavoured rhythm.
songs.preview: Memories of loved ones and of the faith they passed on return unbidden and bring comfort in the night.

songs.title: Maybe Someday
songs.note: A Dylan original from Knocked Out Loaded, a fast, crowded rock song with backing singers, one of the few songs on the album he wrote alone.
songs.preview: A spurned lover imagines that someday his former partner will understand what she gave up, though he hardly believes it.

songs.title: Got My Mind Made Up
songs.note: Co-written by Dylan and Tom Petty and recorded with Petty and the Heartbreakers, with whom Dylan was touring in 1986.
songs.preview: A man has decided to leave, and nothing his lover says will talk him out of taking off.

songs.title: Under Your Spell
songs.note: The closing track of Knocked Out Loaded, co-written by Dylan and the pop lyricist Carole Bayer Sager.
songs.preview: A man under a lover's spell is torn between devotion and the need to break away before he is lost.

songs.title: Let's Stick Together
songs.note: Written and first recorded by Wilbert Harrison in 1962, later remade by Bryan Ferry; Dylan's version opens Down in the Groove.
songs.preview: A man urges his wife not to break up their marriage but to stay together for better or worse.

songs.title: When Did You Leave Heaven?
songs.note: A 1936 popular song by Richard Whiting with words by Walter Bullock, introduced in a Hollywood film; Dylan sings it as a slow, crooning ballad.
songs.preview: An admirer marvels at a woman so lovely that she must have come down from heaven, and wonders how.

songs.title: Sally Sue Brown
songs.note: A rhythm and blues song first recorded by Arthur Alexander, who co-wrote it; Dylan cut it with a rowdy rock band for Down in the Groove.
songs.preview: A man is completely smitten with a girl called Sally Sue Brown and can think of nothing and no one else.
songs.wordsBy: Arthur Alexander, Earl Montgomery and Tom Stafford

songs.title: Had a Dream About You, Baby
songs.note: A Dylan original written for the 1987 film Hearts of Fire, in which he also acted, and included on Down in the Groove.
songs.preview: A man cannot shake the dream he had about a woman and is restless with wanting her.

songs.title: Ugliest Girl in the World
songs.note: Music by Dylan with words by Robert Hunter, the Grateful Dead lyricist, one of two Hunter collaborations on Down in the Groove.
songs.preview: A man cheerfully admits his girlfriend is no beauty, yet he is devoted to her and cannot live without her.

songs.title: Ninety Miles an Hour (Down a Dead End Street)
songs.note: A country song by Hal Blair and Don Robertson, recorded by Hank Snow in 1963; Dylan sings it as a slow, hushed duet-style ballad.
songs.preview: Two people know their forbidden affair can only end badly, yet they keep racing toward it anyway.

songs.title: Shenandoah
songs.note: A traditional American folk song dating from the nineteenth century, often sung as a sea shanty; it closes Down in the Groove.
songs.preview: A wanderer far from home longs for a river, a valley and a love he has left behind across the wide country.

songs.title: Where Teardrops Fall
songs.note: The second track on Oh Mercy, a slow and tender ballad set apart by its soft saxophone and accordion.
songs.preview: A man offers comfort and devotion to someone in a place of sorrow, promising to meet her there.

songs.title: Disease of Conceit
songs.note: A slow, piano-led song near the end of Oh Mercy, close in spirit to a sermon.
songs.preview: Pride is pictured as an epidemic sweeping the land, wrecking lives and blinding people to their own ruin.

songs.title: What Was It You Wanted
songs.note: The ninth and penultimate track on Oh Mercy, a murky, slow-moving song of suspicion with drifting harmonica.
songs.preview: A man keeps asking someone what they really want from him, never quite trusting the answer.

songs.title: Unbelievable
songs.note: The third track on Under the Red Sky, a brisk rock song issued as a single from the album.
songs.preview: A narrator marvels at a world where greed and wrongdoing go unpunished and nothing makes sense anymore.

songs.title: T.V. Talkin' Song
songs.note: The fifth track on Under the Red Sky, a story song delivered in a half-spoken style over a loping groove.
songs.preview: At a London speakers' corner, a man rails against television until the crowd turns ugly and the scene ends up on the news.

songs.title: 10,000 Men
songs.note: The sixth track on Under the Red Sky, a slow blues built from repeated, nursery-rhyme style lines.
songs.preview: An army of ten thousand men passes by in a series of strange, fable-like images.

songs.title: 2 X 2
songs.note: The seventh track on Under the Red Sky, a counting song that echoes the story of Noah's ark.
songs.preview: Pairs, then larger groups, march forward in a counting rhyme that hints at the flood and the end of things.

songs.title: God Knows
songs.note: The eighth track on Under the Red Sky, a song of faith that builds from quiet to a full band.
songs.preview: The singer finds comfort in the belief that God sees everything, including the troubles between people.

songs.title: Handy Dandy
songs.note: The ninth track on Under the Red Sky, a character sketch carried by a prominent organ and a swinging band groove.
songs.preview: A portrait of a charming, careless man surrounded by admirers, whose easy life hides something hollow.

songs.title: Cat's in the Well
songs.note: The closing track of Under the Red Sky, a driving blues that ends the album on an apocalyptic note.
songs.preview: A nursery-rhyme image of a cat in a well opens a vision of a world sliding toward ruin.

songs.title: Jim Jones
songs.note: A traditional Australian convict ballad, the second track on Good as I Been to You, sung over intricate fingerpicked guitar.
songs.preview: A convict sentenced to transportation to Australia vows to break free and take revenge on his jailers.

songs.title: Blackjack Davey
songs.note: A version of the old British ballad also known as Gypsy Davy, the third track on Good as I Been to You.
songs.preview: A married woman leaves her home and husband to ride away with a wandering gypsy.

songs.title: Canadee-i-o
songs.note: A traditional sailing ballad, the fourth track on Good as I Been to You, performed with voice and fingerpicked guitar.
songs.preview: A young woman disguises herself as a sailor to cross the sea, and wins a surprising fortune.

songs.title: Sittin’ on Top of the World
songs.note: A blues first recorded by the Mississippi Sheiks in 1930, which Dylan sings solo on Good as I Been to You.
songs.preview: A man whose lover has left him insists he is doing just fine without her.

songs.title: Little Maggie
songs.note: A traditional Appalachian song, usually played on banjo, that Dylan adapts to solo guitar on Good as I Been to You.
songs.preview: A man watches the woman he loves drink, gamble and give her heart to someone else.

songs.title: Hard Times
songs.note: Stephen Foster wrote this parlour song, known in full as "Hard Times Come Again No More", in the 1850s.
songs.preview: A plea on behalf of the poor and suffering, asking that hard times stop coming back.

songs.title: Step It Up and Go
songs.note: An upbeat Piedmont blues associated with Blind Boy Fuller, one of the liveliest tracks on Good as I Been to You.
songs.preview: A good-humoured blues full of comic scenes, urging everyone to quicken their step and get moving.

songs.title: Tomorrow Night
songs.note: Written by Sam Coslow and Will Grosz in 1939, it became a hit for Lonnie Johnson and was later recorded by Elvis Presley.
songs.preview: A lover wonders whether tonight's tenderness will still be there tomorrow.

songs.title: You’re Gonna Quit Me
songs.note: A country blues recorded by Blind Blake in the 1920s, sung by Dylan with guitar on Good as I Been to You.
songs.preview: A man senses that the woman he loves is about to leave him and asks her not to.

songs.title: Diamond Joe
songs.note: A traditional cowboy song, near the end of Good as I Been to You, which Dylan also sang in the film Masked and Anonymous.
songs.preview: A hired hand complains about working for a stingy, cruel boss and longs to get away from him.

songs.title: Love Henry
songs.note: A traditional murder ballad descended from the old British ballad known as "Young Hunting", it is the second track on World Gone Wrong.
songs.preview: A jealous woman kills the man who means to leave her for another, and a bird witnesses the crime.

songs.title: Ragged & Dirty
songs.note: A country blues sung to his own acoustic guitar, it is the third track on World Gone Wrong.
songs.preview: A down-and-out man, turned away and left with nothing, asks a woman to take him in anyway.

songs.title: Blood in My Eyes
songs.note: A song first recorded by the Mississippi Sheiks in the early 1930s; Dylan's version on World Gone Wrong was given a black-and-white video filmed in London.
songs.preview: A man burns with desire for a woman and keeps trying to win her, even as she slips away.

songs.title: Broke Down Engine
songs.note: A blues by Blind Willie McTell, who recorded it in the early 1930s; Dylan sings it alone with acoustic guitar on World Gone Wrong.
songs.preview: A man compares himself to a worn-out engine that no longer runs, abandoned and begging his woman to return.

songs.title: Two Soldiers
songs.note: A traditional song from the time of the American Civil War, sung by Dylan to acoustic guitar on World Gone Wrong.
songs.preview: Two young soldiers, one leaving people behind and one with no one, march into battle, and neither returns.

songs.title: Jack‐a‐Roe
songs.note: An old ballad, also known as Jackaroe, that Joan Baez and the Grateful Dead also recorded; it is the second-to-last track on World Gone Wrong.
songs.preview: A wealthy merchant's daughter disguises herself as a man and follows her sweetheart to war.

songs.title: Lone Pilgrim
songs.note: An old American hymn that Doc Watson had recorded, it closes World Gone Wrong.
songs.preview: A traveler finds the grave of a pilgrim who died far from home, and the dead man speaks of peace.

songs.title: Dirt Road Blues
songs.note: The second track on Time Out of Mind, a short, rockabilly-tinged shuffle that follows the opener "Love Sick".
songs.preview: A man walks a dusty road looking for a lost love, hoping something will change.

songs.title: Million Miles
songs.note: A slow, smoky blues near the middle of Time Out of Mind, the album's fourth track.
songs.preview: A man feels endlessly far from the woman he loves, even as he tries to get closer.

songs.title: 'til I Fell in Love With You
songs.note: A heavy, stomping blues that is the sixth track on Time Out of Mind.
songs.preview: A man says love has wrecked him, leaving him sleepless, sick and unable to go on as before.

songs.title: Can't Wait
songs.note: A slow, brooding blues near the end of Time Out of Mind; alternate versions were later released on Tell Tale Signs.
songs.preview: A man consumed by longing for a woman says he cannot keep waiting for her much longer.

songs.title: Bye and Bye
songs.note: A light, crooning swing number, the fourth track on "Love and Theft", in the style of prewar popular song.
songs.preview: A man woos a woman in a gentle, easygoing way, though a hint of menace hides under the charm.

songs.title: Lonesome Day Blues
songs.note: A long, driving electric blues, the fifth track on "Love and Theft".
songs.preview: A lonely, embittered man moves through a bleak day, nursing grief and threatening those who wronged him.

songs.title: Floater (Too Much to Ask)
songs.note: A gently swinging song on "Love and Theft" that later drew attention for borrowing lines from Junichi Saga's book Confessions of a Yakuza.
songs.preview: An aging man drifts through memories of family, love and small-town life with dry, rambling humor.

songs.title: Moonlight
songs.note: A soft, old-fashioned crooner's ballad, the eighth track on "Love and Theft".
songs.preview: A man gently invites a woman to come and meet him under the moon.

songs.title: Cry a While
songs.note: A blues near the end of "Love and Theft" that switches between a slow, swaggering pace and a fast, driving shuffle.
songs.preview: A man who once wept over a woman now tells her it is her turn to suffer.

songs.title: Beyond the Horizon
songs.note: A lilting love song on Modern Times whose melody draws on the 1930s popular song "Red Sails in the Sunset".
songs.preview: A man promises that love and peace wait somewhere past the horizon, beyond the troubles of now.

songs.title: Nettie Moore
songs.note: A slow, solemn song on Modern Times whose refrain draws on the 1857 parlour song "Gentle Nettie Moore".
songs.preview: A man mourns a lost love while moving through a hard, disordered world of trouble and judgment.

songs.title: The Levee’s Gonna Break
songs.note: A rocking blues on Modern Times based on "When the Levee Breaks", the 1929 song by Kansas Joe McCoy and Memphis Minnie.
songs.preview: A man warns that the floodwaters are rising and the levee is about to give way.

songs.title: Do You Hear What I Hear?
songs.note: Written in 1962 by Noël Regney and Gloria Shayne as a plea for peace during the Cuban missile crisis, it is the second track on Christmas in the Heart.
songs.preview: News of a newborn child passes from the night wind to a lamb, a shepherd and a king, until it reaches everyone.

songs.title: Winter Wonderland
songs.note: A 1934 standard with words by Richard B. Smith and music by Felix Bernard, here played as a bright, bouncy number early on Christmas in the Heart.
songs.preview: A couple walks through a snowy landscape, building a snowman and dreaming happily about their future together.

songs.title: Hark the Herald Angels Sing
songs.note: An eighteenth-century hymn with words by Charles Wesley, sung to a melody adapted from Felix Mendelssohn, it is one of the album's traditional carols.
songs.preview: Angels announce the birth of Christ and call on every nation to join their song of praise.

songs.title: I'll Be Home for Christmas
songs.note: Written in 1943 by Kim Gannon and Walter Kent and made famous by Bing Crosby, it spoke for soldiers away from home during the Second World War.
songs.preview: Someone far away promises to come home for the holiday, then admits it may only happen in a dream.

songs.title: Little Drummer Boy
songs.note: A carol written by Katherine Kennison Davis in 1941 and popularised by the Harry Simeone Chorale, it sits near the middle of Christmas in the Heart.
songs.preview: A poor boy with nothing to give the newborn Christ offers the only gift he has: his drumming.

songs.title: O' Come All Ye Faithful (Adeste Fideles)
songs.note: An old Latin hymn, usually credited to John Francis Wade in the eighteenth century, which Dylan sings partly in Latin before switching to English.
songs.preview: The faithful are invited to come to Bethlehem, see the newborn Christ and worship him.

songs.title: Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas
songs.note: Written by Hugh Martin and Ralph Blane for the 1944 film Meet Me in St. Louis, where Judy Garland sang it, it became a holiday standard.
songs.preview: A wish that this Christmas may be bright, with troubles set aside and friends gathered close again.

songs.title: Silver Bells
songs.note: Written by Jay Livingston and Ray Evans for the 1951 film The Lemon Drop Kid, it is a Christmas song about the city rather than the countryside.
songs.preview: Busy city streets fill with shoppers, lights and the sound of bells as Christmas draws near.

songs.title: The First Noel
songs.note: A traditional English carol of uncertain age, first printed in the early nineteenth century, sung here with a choir late in Christmas in the Heart.
songs.preview: Shepherds watch their flocks and wise men follow a star to find the newborn king.

songs.title: Christmas Island
songs.note: Written by Lyle Moraine and recorded in 1946 by the Andrews Sisters with Guy Lombardo, it is a lighthearted island novelty near the end of the album.
songs.preview: The singer invites someone to spend Christmas on a tropical island, swapping snow for sunshine and palm trees.

songs.title: The Christmas Song
songs.note: Written in 1945 by Mel Tormé and Bob Wells and made famous by Nat King Cole, it is the penultimate track on Christmas in the Heart.
songs.preview: Familiar winter comforts and children's excitement make up a simple, warm wish for a merry Christmas.

songs.title: O' Little Town of Bethlehem
songs.note: A hymn written by Phillips Brooks in 1868, it closes Christmas in the Heart on a quiet, reverent note.
songs.preview: A quiet town sleeps under the stars on the night a holy child is born there.

songs.title: My Wife's Home Town
songs.note: Written with Robert Hunter and credited also to Willie Dixon, since it is built on his blues "I Just Want to Make Love to You".
songs.preview: A man grumbles, half in jest, that his wife's home town is the root of all his troubles.

songs.title: If You Ever Go to Houston
songs.note: Written with Robert Hunter, it is a mid-tempo Texas song driven by accordion, the album's border-town sound at its plainest.
songs.preview: A traveler offers advice to anyone heading to Houston and other Texas towns, remembering people and places he knew.

songs.title: Forgetful Heart
songs.note: Written with Robert Hunter, it is a slow, minor-key ballad and one of the darkest songs on Together Through Life.
songs.preview: A man speaks to his own heart, which has let go of a love he still cannot forget.

songs.title: Jolene
songs.note: Written with Robert Hunter and not the Dolly Parton song of the same name, it is a stomping blues number in the middle of the album.
songs.preview: A swaggering man declares his devotion to a woman named Jolene and boasts of his own power.

songs.title: This Dream of You
songs.note: The only song on Together Through Life that Dylan wrote without Robert Hunter, it has a Tex-Mex lilt with accordion and violin.
songs.preview: A lonely man clings to a dream of the woman he loves, the one thing keeping him going.

songs.title: Shake Shake Mama
songs.note: Written with Robert Hunter, it is a raw, fast blues shuffle in the second half of Together Through Life.
songs.preview: A restless man urges a woman to dance and shake, mixing lust with grumbling about his troubles.

songs.title: It's All Good
songs.note: Written with Robert Hunter, it closes Together Through Life with a jaunty tune that turns a cheerful catchphrase into irony.
songs.preview: Amid broken homes, corruption and decay, the singer keeps insisting with a straight face that everything is fine.

songs.title: Soon After Midnight
songs.note: The second track on Tempest, a slow and gentle ballad with a lilting, old-fashioned doo-wop feel.
songs.preview: A late-night love song from a man who sounds tender and patient, though a quiet menace keeps slipping in.

songs.title: Narrow Way
songs.note: The third track on Tempest, a long, hard-driving blues built on a repeating riff.
songs.preview: A weary, stubborn man insists that one day he and the woman he wants will finally meet halfway.

songs.title: Long and Wasted Years
songs.note: The fourth track on Tempest, a mid-tempo song delivered in a rough, half-spoken voice over a circling guitar figure.
songs.preview: A man talks to a former partner about the years they let slip away and the distance now between them.

songs.title: Pay in Blood
songs.note: The fifth track on Tempest, a snarling mid-tempo rocker driven by piano and guitar.
songs.preview: A furious, vengeful voice declares that he settles every debt with violence rather than with money.

songs.title: Scarlet Town
songs.note: The sixth track on Tempest; Scarlet Town is the setting of the old ballad "Barbara Allen".
songs.preview: A portrait of a decaying, haunted town where love, sin and death sit side by side.

songs.title: Early Roman Kings
songs.note: The seventh track on Tempest, a heavy blues built on the stop-time riff familiar from Muddy Waters' "Mannish Boy".
songs.preview: A swaggering portrait of brutal, powerful men who rule by force and fear no one.

songs.title: Tin Angel
songs.note: The eighth track on Tempest, a long narrative ballad that runs for roughly nine minutes.
songs.preview: A husband pursues his runaway wife and her lover, and the confrontation ends in death for all three.

songs.title: The Night We Called It a Day
songs.note: Written by Matt Dennis and Tom Adair in 1941 and recorded by Frank Sinatra in 1942; the second track on Shadows in the Night.
songs.preview: A lover remembers the night a romance ended and how the whole world seemed to darken with it.

songs.title: Stay With Me
songs.note: Written by Jerome Moross and Carolyn Leigh for the 1963 film "The Cardinal" and recorded by Frank Sinatra; the third track on Shadows in the Night.
songs.preview: A humble prayer asking God for guidance, comfort and companionship through doubt and darkness.

songs.title: Autumn Leaves
songs.note: A French song by Joseph Kosma and Jacques Prévert, with English words by Johnny Mercer; the fourth track on Shadows in the Night.
songs.preview: Falling leaves in autumn bring back memories of a summer love that is now gone for good.

songs.title: Why Try to Change Me Now
songs.note: Written by Cy Coleman and Joseph McCarthy and recorded by Frank Sinatra in 1952; the fifth track on Shadows in the Night.
songs.preview: A dreamy, unconventional man asks the woman he loves to accept him as he is rather than reform him.

songs.title: Some Enchanted Evening
songs.note: Written by Richard Rodgers and Oscar Hammerstein II for the 1949 Broadway musical "South Pacific"; the sixth track on Shadows in the Night.
songs.preview: Advice to seize love the moment you meet it, because such a chance may never come again.

songs.title: Where Are You?
songs.note: Written by Jimmy McHugh and Harold Adamson in 1937 and the title song of a 1957 Frank Sinatra album; eighth on Shadows in the Night.
songs.preview: An abandoned lover asks where the one who left has gone and why their love came to nothing.

songs.title: What'll I Do
songs.note: Written by Irving Berlin in 1923 and recorded by Frank Sinatra; the ninth track on Shadows in the Night.
songs.preview: A lonely lover wonders how to go on now that the person who mattered most is gone.

songs.title: Maybe You'll Be There
songs.note: A 1940s ballad by Rube Bloom and Sammy Gallop; the second track on Fallen Angels.
songs.preview: A lonely singer clings to the hope that a lost love might be waiting somewhere ahead.

songs.title: Polka Dots and Moonbeams
songs.note: Written by Jimmy Van Heusen and Johnny Burke in 1940 and recorded by Frank Sinatra with Tommy Dorsey; the third track on Fallen Angels.
songs.preview: A sweet story of a young man meeting a girl at a country dance and falling in love.

songs.title: Skylark
songs.note: Written by Hoagy Carmichael with words by Johnny Mercer in 1941; the fifth track on Fallen Angels.
songs.preview: A lonely singer asks a skylark whether it has seen anywhere the love they are longing for.

songs.title: Nevertheless
songs.note: Written by Bert Kalmar and Harry Ruby in 1931 and recorded by Frank Sinatra in 1950; the sixth track on Fallen Angels.
songs.preview: Someone admits that falling in love may end badly, but chooses to fall anyway.

songs.title: All or Nothing at All
songs.note: Written by Arthur Altman and Jack Lawrence and first recorded by Frank Sinatra with Harry James in 1939; the seventh track on Fallen Angels.
songs.preview: A lover refuses to settle for half a romance: it must be complete devotion or nothing.

songs.title: On a Little Street in Singapore
songs.note: Written by Peter DeRose and Billy Hill in 1938 and recorded by Frank Sinatra with Harry James; the eighth track on Fallen Angels.
songs.preview: A secret romance unfolds in a far-off port city, where two lovers meet in hiding.

songs.title: It Had to Be You
songs.note: Written by Isham Jones and Gus Kahn in 1924, one of the most recorded songs of its era; the ninth track on Fallen Angels.
songs.preview: Only one person, flaws and all, could ever win this singer's heart.

songs.title: That Old Black Magic
songs.note: Written by Harold Arlen and Johnny Mercer for the 1942 film "Star Spangled Rhythm"; the eleventh track on Fallen Angels.
songs.preview: Falling in love feels like being under a spell the singer cannot and does not want to break.

songs.title: Come Rain or Come Shine
songs.note: Written by Harold Arlen and Johnny Mercer for the 1946 Broadway musical "St. Louis Woman"; it closes Fallen Angels.
songs.preview: A promise of lasting love, whatever luck, weather or fortune may bring to the couple.

songs.title: I Guess I’ll Have to Change My Plans
songs.note: Written by Arthur Schwartz and Howard Dietz in 1929, it opens the first of Triplicate's three discs.
songs.preview: A man who had his future mapped out with someone learns she is gone and must start over.

songs.title: I Could Have Told You
songs.note: A torch ballad from the 1950s songbook that Frank Sinatra recorded, sitting early on the first disc of Triplicate.
songs.preview: Someone who watched a lover leave says he saw it coming all along and was hurt anyway.

songs.title: Once Upon a Time
songs.note: Written by Charles Strouse and Lee Adams for the 1962 Broadway musical All American, later recorded by Tony Bennett and Frank Sinatra.
songs.preview: An older man remembers a youthful, carefree love and the world it belonged to, both now long gone.

songs.title: This Nearly Was Mine
songs.note: A Rodgers and Hammerstein song from South Pacific (1949), where the French planter Emile de Becque sings it; here a slow waltz on Triplicate.
songs.preview: A man mourns a love he held almost in his hands before it slipped away.

songs.title: That Old Feeling
songs.note: Written by Sammy Fain and Lew Brown in 1937 for the film Vogues of 1938, it became a standard sung by many jazz and pop singers.
songs.preview: Seeing a former love again, a man finds the old attraction comes straight back.

songs.title: It Gets Lonely Early
songs.note: Written by Jimmy Van Heusen and Sammy Cahn and recorded by Frank Sinatra on his 1965 album September of My Years.
songs.preview: A man living alone after a breakup finds the evenings start too soon and stretch too long.

songs.title: My One and Only Love
songs.note: Written by Guy Wood and Robert Mellin in the early 1950s, famously recorded by Frank Sinatra and later by John Coltrane with Johnny Hartman.
songs.preview: A man tells the woman he loves that she is the only one, and describes how she moves him.

songs.title: Trade Winds
songs.note: Written by Cliff Friend and Charles Tobias and a 1940 hit for Bing Crosby; it closes the first disc of Triplicate.
songs.preview: On a tropical shore, the warm winds bring back memories of a lover who is no longer there.

songs.title: Braggin’
songs.note: A little-known 1940s swing number, Braggin' opens the second disc of Triplicate at a jaunty tempo.
songs.preview: A man playfully boasts about his sweetheart while admitting he may be bragging a bit too much.

songs.title: Imagination
songs.note: Written by Jimmy Van Heusen and Johnny Burke in 1940, it was a hit for the Tommy Dorsey Orchestra with Frank Sinatra and for Glenn Miller.
songs.preview: A man reflects on how the imagination can make a lover seem perfect, and wonders if it is fooling him.

songs.title: How Deep Is the Ocean
songs.note: Written by Irving Berlin in 1932, it has been recorded by countless singers and is one of his best-known ballads.
songs.preview: A lover answers the question of how much he cares by pointing to the depth of the sea and the height of the sky.

songs.title: P.S. I Love You
songs.note: Written by Gordon Jenkins with words by Johnny Mercer in 1934; not the Beatles song of the same name.
songs.preview: A man away from home writes a letter to the woman he loves, filling it with small news and his longing.

songs.title: The Best Is Yet to Come
songs.note: Written by Cy Coleman and Carolyn Leigh in 1959 and made famous by Frank Sinatra with Count Basie's orchestra in 1964.
songs.preview: A man courting someone promises that their romance has only just begun and its best days lie ahead.

songs.title: But Beautiful
songs.note: Written by Jimmy Van Heusen and Johnny Burke for the 1947 Bing Crosby and Bob Hope film Road to Rio.
songs.preview: Love is described as a tangle of opposites, funny and sad, calm and wild, but always beautiful.

songs.title: Here’s That Rainy Day
songs.note: Written by Jimmy Van Heusen and Johnny Burke for the 1953 Broadway musical Carnival in Flanders, later a jazz standard.
songs.preview: Someone who once laughed off talk of hard times finds that the hard times have finally arrived.

songs.title: Where Is the One
songs.note: Written by Alec Wilder and Edwin Finckel and recorded by Frank Sinatra on his 1957 album Where Are You?
songs.preview: A lonely man asks where the person meant for him is, and whether he will ever find her.

songs.title: There’s a Flaw in My Flue
songs.note: Written by Jimmy Van Heusen and Johnny Burke; Frank Sinatra recorded it in 1956, and it closes the second disc of Triplicate.
songs.preview: A man alone by a smoky fireplace keeps seeing the face of a lost love whenever the chimney acts up.

songs.title: Day In, Day Out
songs.note: Written by Rube Bloom with words by Johnny Mercer in 1939, it opens the third disc of Triplicate.
songs.preview: Every day the same overwhelming feeling returns, the thrill of being in love that never wears off.

songs.title: I Couldn’t Sleep a Wink Last Night
songs.note: Written by Jimmy McHugh and Harold Adamson for Higher and Higher (1943), a film in which Frank Sinatra sang it.
songs.preview: After a quarrel with his sweetheart, a man lies awake all night until he can set things right.

songs.title: Sentimental Journey
songs.note: Written by Les Brown, Ben Homer and Bud Green; Doris Day's 1945 recording with Les Brown's band became a symbol of soldiers coming home.
songs.preview: A traveller sets off by train for home, eager to return to the places and people of the past.

songs.title: Somewhere Along the Way
songs.note: Written by Kurt Adams with words by Sammy Gallop; Nat King Cole had a hit with it in 1952.
songs.preview: A man realises that at some point on the road of life he lost the person he loved.

songs.title: When the World Was Young
songs.note: Based on a French song by Philippe-Gérard, with English words by Johnny Mercer; Frank Sinatra and Peggy Lee recorded it.
songs.preview: A worldly, older man looks back with longing on the innocent days of his youth.

songs.title: These Foolish Things
songs.note: Written in 1936 by Jack Strachey with words by Eric Maschwitz, it is a British song that became an American standard.
songs.preview: Small everyday objects and moments keep reminding a man of a lover who is gone.

songs.title: You Go to My Head
songs.note: Written by J. Fred Coots with words by Haven Gillespie in 1938, it was recorded by Billie Holiday and many others.
songs.preview: A lover compares the giddy effect of the person he adores to being intoxicated.

songs.title: Stardust
songs.note: Hoagy Carmichael's 1927 melody, later given words by Mitchell Parish, became one of the most recorded songs of the century; Dylan sings it near the end of Triplicate.
songs.preview: Alone at nightfall, a man remembers a love that has ended and finds the memory itself is all he has left.

songs.title: It’s Funny to Everyone but Me
songs.note: A 1939 ballad by Jack Lawrence, recorded early on by Frank Sinatra with Harry James; Dylan places it next to last on Triplicate.
songs.preview: A man whose heart has been broken notices that his misery amuses everyone around him except himself.

songs.title: Why Was I Born
songs.note: Written by Jerome Kern and Oscar Hammerstein II for the 1929 Broadway show Sweet Adeline, it closes Triplicate and with it Dylan's run of standards albums.
songs.preview: Someone devoted to a lover who does not return the feeling asks what the point of their own life can be.

songs.title: I’ve Made Up My Mind to Give Myself to You
songs.note: The fourth track on Rough and Rowdy Ways, a gentle, slow love song that stands apart from the darker, wordier pieces around it.
songs.preview: An older man, having travelled and seen enough, decides calmly to commit himself completely to the one he loves.

songs.title: Black Rider
songs.note: The fifth track on Rough and Rowdy Ways, one of the sparest arrangements on the album, built mostly on quiet guitar.
songs.preview: A man speaks to a dark, shadowy rider who stalks him and tells him to keep his distance.

songs.title: Mother of Muses
songs.note: The seventh track on Rough and Rowdy Ways, a slow hymn-like invocation of the muse that also salutes Second World War generals.
songs.preview: An aging singer calls on the mother of the muses for inspiration and honours those who fought and marched before him.

songs.title: The Mighty Quinn (Quinn the Eskimo)
songs.note: Written during the 1967 Basement Tapes sessions and a 1968 hit for Manfred Mann; Self Portrait has it live from the 1969 Isle of Wight festival with the Band.
songs.preview: Everyone is restless and stuck until the mysterious Quinn arrives, and then the whole crowd comes joyfully alive.

songs.title: Minstrel Boy
songs.note: A Dylan song from the 1967 basement period, not the old Irish ballad; Self Portrait's version is live from the 1969 Isle of Wight festival with the Band.
songs.preview: A worn-out travelling minstrel keeps rolling on, and the song asks whether anyone will help or reward him.
